title: An object matching neither BidRequest nor BidResponse shape on either side is honestly unrecognized

replaceRequest.note: neither a BidRequest nor a BidResponse

replaceResponse.note: neither a BidRequest nor a BidResponse

specNotes: OpenRTB 2.6 §3.2.1 defines BidRequest as an object carrying at minimum `id` and a non-empty `imp[]`; §4.2.1 defines BidResponse as an object carrying at minimum `id` and either `seatbid[]` or `nbr`. A plain object with unrelated keys satisfies neither shape and is not a documented vendor dialect shape either, so both sides must be reported as unrecognized, not silently accepted as one or the other.

detectType() checks `imp[]`, `seatbid[]`, the 3.0 envelope, the vendor-feed heuristics and the malformed-payload site/app/device and id+cur/bidid/nbr heuristics in order; an object with neither `id` nor any of those signals matches none of them, so both sides fall through to `payload.unknown_type` rather than being misclassified as one or the other.

Crosscheck is asked to compare two objects that are neither a valid request nor a valid response; it must refuse with `crosscheck.no_request` rather than inventing a per-bid verdict against an empty seatbid or an empty imp list.

A literal `{}` on both sides was considered instead, but the real HTTP contract (modules/analyze/handler.js, `hasReq`/`hasRes` computed as `Object.keys(x).length > 0`) treats `{}` as indistinguishable from 'nothing submitted' and returns a deliberate, documented 400 `empty_payload` (the in-code comment reads: 'Empty payload is now an explicit 400 instead of a synthetic unknown_type finding masquerading as a real validation error') — a sensible product decision, not a defect, but one that would prevent this case from ever exercising Core's own `payload.unknown_type` path at the HTTP layer. A small non-empty object that still matches no recognized shape exercises the same Core behavior while keeping `hasReq`/`hasRes` true, so the 200 pipeline (and the crosscheck refusal) is what actually runs end to end.
